title: Mian Mir
hookLine: a Sufi saint of Lahore who was Guru Arjan's friend; tradition says he laid the Harmandir's foundation stone

lines: A ROLL CALL OF THE WEEK.
THE LAST FACE ISN'T A SIKH.
cards: The week ends here, so first, a roll call of the faces around the Gurus. Baba Buddha, who served Guru after Guru. Bibi Amro, singing at the churn.
Bibi Bhani, her hand under a broken stool. Mata Ganga, walking with plain bread. Bhai Gurdas, the scribe who ran and came back.
Bhai Bidhi Chand, over the wall. Every one a Sikh, or a Guru's family. And the last face of the week, standing beside Guru Arjan at the edge of a pool in Amritsar, isn't a Sikh at all.

teach.b: Mian Mir was a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, who lived in Lahore. Tradition remembers him for a plain life of prayer and for the company he kept, which included Guru Arjan.
They were friends: not allies in a debate, not rivals being polite, but friends who visited and talked about God.

teach.h: TRADITION: HE LAID THE FIRST STONE.
teach.b: When Guru Arjan was building the Harmandir, the house of God in the middle of the pool at Amritsar, tradition says he invited Mian Mir to lay its foundation stone. Some historians question whether it happened that way.
Sikhs still tell it, and it's easy to hear why: a Sikh house of worship, its first stone set by a Muslim friend. That fits the building itself.
The Harmandir sits low, so you step down to enter it, and it has doors on every side, open to anyone coming from any direction. There's a harder story too.
When Guru Arjan was arrested and tortured in Lahore, tradition says Mian Mir came to him, grieving, and offered to intervene.
Guru Arjan, the story says, asked him not to: this was God's will, and he accepted it. Mian Mir stayed a friend to the end, and the Guru stayed himself. Neither man became the other.

Mian Mir didn't become a Sikh; Guru Arjan didn't become a Sufi. Each stood fully in his own path, and they were close anyway. Sikhs remember Mian Mir with honor, and his shrine in Lahore is still visited.

how: Sikhs remember Mian Mir with honor as Guru Arjan's friend, and the story that he laid the Harmandir's foundation stone is often told at the Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple) in Amritsar.

games.q: you're Mian Mir. your friend Guru Arjan has been arrested in Lahore, and you go to him, grieving, offering to intervene. what does tradition say he answers?
o: yes, use your influence to free me.
no, this is God's will, and I accept it.
stay away, for your own safety.
games.why: tradition says Guru Arjan asked him not to intervene and accepted it as God's will; Mian Mir stayed his friend to the end.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose path is different from yours: another faith, no faith, or a different way within the same one.

See their face, and remember one time they were good to you, or good company, or just there; let that memory sit without explaining your differences. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, and let them be in it.

wordCard.voice: Mian Mir. A Sufi of Lahore, Guru Arjan's friend, who, tradition says, laid the foundation stone of the Harmandir.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Mian Mir; Mian is a title of respect, here for a Sufi saint.

carryVoice: Your line: friends across faiths. Nobody was asked to switch. Eight hundred twelve days, and counting.
